symptom_description: OEE is below the client's configured threshold.
root_cause_framework: TPM Six Big Losses (breakdowns, setup/adjustment, idling/minor stops, reduced speed, startup defects, process defects)
diagnostic_steps: Check whether Availability, Performance, and Quality are stored as separate columns before promising a factor-level decomposition — today's oee_pct column may be pre-calculated without the three components broken out (see the oee KPI card's formula note).
If decomposable: identify which of the three factors has moved most versus its own trailing baseline.
For an Availability-driven gap: pull the stoppage reason-code breakdown for the same period and classify against the six big losses.

For a Performance-driven gap: check changeover_time and hourly_shift_output for the same equipment/line — but see that KPI's data-quality note on the hardcoded 64-unit target before trusting the percentage at face value.
For a Quality-driven gap: cross-reference eol_defect_rate and scrap_rate for the same period.

recommended_actions.action: Route to maintenance log review for the specific equipment_id; cross-check maintenance_alerts for the same equipment in the prior period for an early warning that was missed.
Review changeover_time trend for the same line; consider a SMED-style internal/external setup-step review if changeover time itself is the driver.
Check eol_defect_rate specifically in the first units after a changeover, since startup losses are a distinct TPM loss category from steady-state quality issues.

symptom_description: A scrap, rework, or COPQ metric has spiked relative to its baseline.
root_cause_framework: Fishbone / 5M (Machine, Method, Material, Man, Measurement) + 5-Why
diagnostic_steps: Pull the Top 5 Scrap Reason Codes for the affected period — remember avg_unit_cost falls back to a hardcoded $45.50/unit if mfg_cost_usd or units_produced is missing, so confirm those columns are populated before trusting the cost figure.
Run a 5-Why pass against the top reason code, structured across the 5M categories, before changing any process parameter.
Check whether the spike is isolated to one shift, one machine, or one material lot before assuming a systemic process issue.
Cross-check CAPA Closure Time — a rising closure time alongside a scrap spike suggests a repeat cause that wasn't actually closed out last time.

recommended_actions.action: Cross-check the affected lot/batch against incoming-material inspection records before adjusting the process.
Check tooling/mold cycle-count against its maintenance schedule for the affected equipment_id.
Check whether the spike correlates with a specific shift or a recent operator/training change before treating it as a process problem.

provenance.license_note: Public concept

symptom_description: Average changeover time is trending upward, pressuring schedule attainment or contributing to delayed work orders.
root_cause_framework: SMED (internal vs. external setup steps)
diagnostic_steps: Confirm the trend is genuinely rising (not a single outlier run) using the client's own historical changeover_time series.
Identify whether the same tooling/mold or the same line is disproportionately represented in the recent changeovers.
Distinguish setup steps that require the machine to be stopped (internal) from those that don't (external) for the affected changeover type.
Check delayed_work_orders for the same line to see whether changeover time is already translating into missed dates, not just a slower average.

recommended_actions.action: Identify any external-setup steps currently being done while the machine is stopped, and move them to run in parallel with the prior production run instead.
Check whether the changeover is waiting on tooling/mold retrieval or preparation time, which is a logistics fix, not a process fix.

symptom_description: Schedule attainment / plan adherence is below target, or delayed work orders are rising.
root_cause_framework: Theory of Constraints (identify the binding constraint before acting)
diagnostic_steps: Check capacity_utilization for the affected line — sustained utilization near 100% removes the buffer needed to absorb any variability without a schedule slip.
Check manufacturing_cycle_time trend — a rising cycle time with flat throughput shows up here before it shows up as a WIP Valuation increase.
Check maintenance_alerts and delayed_work_orders for the same period to distinguish an equipment-driven slip from a planning/material-driven one.

recommended_actions.action: Check purchase/supplier data for the same window before assuming a manufacturing-side cause — this is a cross-domain check, not just an internal one.
Cross-reference maintenance_alerts for the affected equipment in the prior period for an early warning that preceded the slip.

provenance.license_note: Public concept

symptom_description: Conversion cost / cost per unit is rising.
root_cause_framework: Cost driver decomposition (volume vs. input cost vs. efficiency)
diagnostic_steps: Check oee for the same period — if OEE is flat while conversion cost rises, the driver is more likely input/material cost than process efficiency.
Check total_production_yield (units produced) — a conversion-cost rise with falling volume can be a fixed-cost absorption effect, not a true efficiency loss.
Check wip_valuation — a build-up in WIP can mean cost is being carried rather than converted, inflating the per-unit figure for the period measured.

recommended_actions.action: Cross-check purchase/procurement data for material price movement in the same window before attributing the rise to a manufacturing-side cause.

symptom_description: Inventory Record Accuracy is falling or Cycle Count Variance is rising.
root_cause_framework: Transaction-discipline root cause (not a physical-count problem first)
diagnostic_steps: Check cycle_count_variance trend first — it is the leading indicator; IRA is the lagging confirmation of the same underlying problem.
Identify whether the variance concentrates in specific SKUs, locations, or shifts before assuming a system-wide issue.
Check whether a system/connector change coincided with the start of the trend (relevant once Epic 1's connector framework is live) — a mapping change can silently break transaction posting.

recommended_actions.action: Audit recent transaction volume by user/shift for the affected SKU/location before assuming a systemic data problem.
Check for a recent connector or mapping change (Epic 1) that could be posting transactions incorrectly.

symptom_description: Predictive maintenance alerts are trending upward for a piece of equipment.
root_cause_framework: TPM — treat rising alerts as the earliest warning stage, before an unplanned breakdown
diagnostic_steps: Check whether the alert count is concentrated on one equipment_id or spread across a line — concentrated points at a specific asset's wear/maintenance schedule.
Cross-check capa_closure_time for any open corrective action on the same equipment — a slow-closing CAPA alongside rising alerts is a compounding risk, not two separate issues.

recommended_actions.action: Escalate to a scheduled maintenance window for the specific equipment_id before it becomes an unplanned breakdown affecting OEE's Availability factor.

symptom_description: An in-process control-limit deviation or batch-record discrepancy has been flagged in a pharmaceutical production run.
root_cause_framework: FDA cGMP deviation investigation (21 CFR 211.192) — every deviation requires a documented investigation and disposition before the batch can be released, regardless of whether the deviation is ultimately judged to have affected product quality.
diagnostic_steps: Confirm the deviation has an open investigation record before anything else — in a cGMP environment, an undocumented deviation is itself a finding, independent of root cause.

Check whether the deviation is isolated to one batch/lot or recurring across multiple lots on the same line — a recurring deviation escalates from a batch-disposition question to a process-capability (Cpk) question.
Cross-reference first_pass_yield_by_stage for the same batch to see whether the deviation correlates with a specific process stage, not just a specific time.
Check capa_closure_rate history for this line — a pattern of slow CAPA closure alongside recurring deviations suggests a systemic quality-system gap, not an isolated event.

recommended_actions.action: Hold the affected batch pending QA disposition; do not release on the strength of a favorable end-of-line test alone — cGMP requires the investigation to close first.
Cross-check the incoming-material certificate of analysis for the lot in use against historical batches that did not deviate.

provenance.license_note: Public US federal regulation, structural summary only

symptom_description: A process-safety or mechanical-integrity audit finding has been raised at a petroleum/chemical facility.
root_cause_framework: OSHA Process Safety Management (29 CFR 1910.119) — findings are triaged by whether they touch a Highly Hazardous Chemical process, which changes the required closure timeline and escalation path versus a general quality nonconformance.
diagnostic_steps: Classify whether the finding is process-safety-critical (touches a covered process under PSM) or a general quality/housekeeping finding — these follow different closure-time expectations and cannot be averaged together in a single CAPA metric.

For a process-safety-critical finding, check whether an interim safeguard (e.g. increased monitoring, operating-limit tightening) has been put in place while the permanent CAPA is still open — PSM findings are not left unmitigated pending closure.
Cross-check whether this is a recurring finding type across audit cycles — a repeat finding indicates the prior CAPA's corrective action did not address the actual root cause.

recommended_actions.action: Escalate to the mechanical-integrity inspection schedule for the specific asset; check whether the inspection interval itself needs tightening, not just this instance of the finding.

provenance.license_note: Public US federal regulation, structural summary only

symptom_description: Customer Return Rate has moved in a consumer-products context, where returns are a routine retail-channel occurrence rather than an automatic quality-escape signal.
root_cause_framework: ISO 10377 post-market surveillance — the emphasis is on detecting a PATTERN across returns/complaints, not reacting to any single return, since some baseline return rate is expected in this channel.
diagnostic_steps: Segment returns by stated reason code (defect vs. buyer's-remorse vs. wrong-item-ordered) before treating the whole return-rate movement as a quality signal — only the defect-coded segment is actually a COPQ/quality question.

Check whether the movement is concentrated in one SKU/batch or spread across the product line — a single-SKU spike points to a production or packaging issue; a spread-out increase points to a channel or seasonal effect instead.
Cross-reference copq for the same period to see whether rework/return-processing cost is moving with the return rate or independently of it.

recommended_actions.action: Pull the defect-coded return subset specifically and cross-check against the Pareto/scrap-reason data for the same production window.

symptom_description: Maintenance activity for an industrial-products asset is skewing toward corrective (reactive) rather than planned (preventive) work.
root_cause_framework: ISO 55000 Asset Management — a rising corrective-to-planned ratio is treated as a leading indicator of asset-management maturity slipping, not just a maintenance-scheduling inconvenience, since industrial-products equipment is typically higher-cost and longer-lived than high-volume consumer-manufacturing equipment.
diagnostic_steps: Check whether delayed_work_orders is concentrated on preventive-maintenance work orders specifically, versus production work orders — a PM backlog is what actually drives the shift toward reactive maintenance.
Cross-reference maintenance_alerts for the same asset class to see whether alerts are being raised but not converted into scheduled PM work orders in time.

recommended_actions.action: Review the PM scheduling backlog by asset criticality — prioritize closing the backlog on the highest-criticality assets first, not oldest-open-first, per ISO 55000's risk-based asset-management principle.

provenance.license_note: Public concept summary, no reproduction of licensed standard text

symptom_description: An SPC out-of-control point or end-of-line defect has occurred on a characteristic flagged safety-critical or key-product-characteristic (KPC) on an automotive line.
root_cause_framework: 8D Problem Solving — the standard OEM-mandated corrective-action methodology (Ford/GM/Stellantis and most Tier 1 supplier agreements require an 8D, not a generic CAPA form, for a safety-critical or customer-facing quality escape).
diagnostic_steps: Confirm containment (D3) has happened FIRST — in an 8D, containing suspect parts in the field/in-transit/in-plant takes priority over root-cause analysis, unlike a general manufacturing CAPA where investigation typically comes first.
Check whether the characteristic is tagged safety-critical/KPC in the control plan — this determines whether the customer (OEM) must be notified before containment is even complete, not after.

Cross-reference the AIAG Core Tools control plan and the most recent PPAP for this part number — a safety-critical deviation often traces back to a process parameter that drifted outside what PPAP originally validated.
Verify Cpk against the OEM's required threshold for this characteristic (commonly >= 1.67 for safety-critical, not the generic 1.33) before declaring the process back in control.

recommended_actions.action: Stop shipment of suspect parts pending 8D containment (D3) sign-off; do not wait for root cause (D4) before containing.
Re-verify the gauge/measurement system (MSA) before trusting the Cpk number itself — a safety-critical Cpk near the OEM threshold is exactly where measurement error matters most.

provenance.source_name: AIAG Core Tools (APQP/PPAP/FMEA/MSA/SPC) + common OEM 8D requirement

symptom_description: End-of-line defects or scrap have risen on an electronics assembly line (populated board/PCBA).
root_cause_framework: IPC-A-610 defect classification — defects are triaged by Class (1/2/3, reflecting end-use reliability requirement) and by defect type (solder joint, component placement, moisture-sensitive-device handling) before a generic scrap-reason Pareto is useful, since a Class 3 (high-reliability) defect and a cosmetic Class 1 defect are not the same severity even at the same count.
diagnostic_steps: Classify the defect against IPC-A-610's acceptance criteria for the board's assigned Class before adding it to a generic scrap-reason bucket — a Class 3 board held to Class 1 criteria will under-report real defect severity.

Check reflow-oven temperature profile logs for the affected run if the defect is solder-joint-related (cold joint, tombstoning, bridging) — this is the most common root cause IPC-A-610 practitioners check first.

For component-related defects, verify Moisture Sensitive Device (MSD) floor-life/bake-out records for the lot — a common, easily-missed cause of intermittent defects that a simple scrap-reason code won't surface.

recommended_actions.action: Pull the reflow oven's thermal profile for the affected run and compare against the qualified profile for this board — a drifted profile is the single most common root cause of a solder-joint defect spike.
Check floor-life tracking for moisture-sensitive components used in the affected run; re-bake and re-verify before assuming a placement-equipment issue.

provenance.license_note: Public concept summary, no reproduction of licensed IPC standard text

symptom_description: Changeover time or post-changeover scrap/COPQ has risen on an injection molding line.
root_cause_framework: Scientific/Decoupled Molding — isolates variation to one of the three molding phases (fill, pack, hold) before adjusting multiple process parameters at once, which is the most common way a changeover 'fix' actually introduces new variation instead of removing it.
diagnostic_steps: Check whether the variation shows up during fill, pack, or hold phase specifically (via cavity pressure/transfer-position data if available) before changing screw speed, pressure, AND temperature simultaneously — changing one variable at a time is the core Scientific Molding discipline this playbook is named for.

Cross-reference dimension_measurement_mm against the run's LSL/USL immediately after a changeover specifically — startup variation right after a mold/material change is a distinct signal from steady-state drift later in the run.

Confirm the fill-to-pack transfer point wasn't changed as part of the changeover itself — an inconsistent transfer point is one of the most common causes of part-to-part variation this methodology specifically targets.

recommended_actions.action: Verify the fill-to-pack transfer position/pressure against the qualified process setup sheet for this mold before adjusting anything else.
Check the incoming resin lot's melt-flow-index certificate against the lot the process was originally qualified against.

symptom_description: Incoming-material or supplier-attributed defects are pushing a part number's PPM (parts-per-million defect rate) toward or past an OEM supplier-scorecard threshold.
root_cause_framework: AIAG Incoming Inspection / OEM Supplier PPM Scorecard (Ford Q1, GM BIQS) — escalation is scorecard-driven with contractual consequences, not just an internal quality metric.
diagnostic_steps: Confirm whether the defect is attributable to the supplier (incoming material/component) or introduced in-house before escalating to the supplier — check the incoming-inspection record for the specific lot first.
Check whether this is a recurring supplier/part-number combination across multiple periods — a single-lot event and a recurring pattern trigger different OEM-facing escalation paths.
Cross-reference capa_closure_time for any open supplier corrective action on the same part number — a slow-closing supplier CAPA alongside a fresh PPM event compounds the scorecard impact.

recommended_actions.action: Issue a supplier corrective action request (SCAR) referencing the specific lot and defect mode; hold remaining lot inventory pending disposition rather than consuming it into production.
Escalate within the supplier-scorecard governance process — a slow-closing supplier CAPA is itself a scorecard factor independent of the original defect.

symptom_description: End-of-line or field defects on an electronics assembly show an intermittent or delayed-failure pattern inconsistent with a straightforward solder/placement defect.
root_cause_framework: ESD Association ANSI/ESD S20.20 (electrostatic discharge control) + IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 (moisture/reflow sensitivity classification) — targets latent damage that passes initial inspection but fails later, distinct from the immediately-visible defects IPC-A-610 classification catches.
diagnostic_steps: Check whether the failure pattern is immediate (catches at EOL inspection) or delayed/field — a delayed pattern points toward latent ESD or moisture-induced damage rather than a visible solder/placement defect.
Review ESD control-plan compliance (grounding, ionization, handling procedure adherence) for the affected work area and shift before assuming a component-quality issue.

Cross-check MSD floor-life/bake-out records again specifically for LATENT damage signatures (e.g. delamination, popcorning under thermal stress) — this is a different failure mode than the immediate placement defect the solder-defect playbook already checks.

recommended_actions.action: Audit ESD control-plan compliance for the affected workstation/shift; re-verify grounding and ionization equipment calibration before resuming production of ESD-sensitive components.
Cross-check the affected lot's floor-life exposure against J-STD-020 classification limits; quarantine remaining stock from the same lot pending re-bake verification.

symptom_description: Dimensional measurements are drifting out of control limits, or warpage/shrinkage-related scrap is rising, on an injection molding line.
root_cause_framework: Scientific Molding dimensional-stability analysis — isolates whether drift originates from mold cooling uniformity, material shrinkage characteristics, or packing-phase pressure/time, since each requires a different corrective lever.
diagnostic_steps: Confirm the drift is dimensional (warpage/shrinkage) and not a cosmetic or strength defect before applying this playbook — different root-cause families apply to each.

Check mold cooling-channel temperature uniformity for the affected cavity/mold — uneven cooling is one of the most common warpage root causes and is distinct from a fill/pack/hold process-parameter issue.

Verify the incoming resin lot's shrinkage-rate specification (per ASTM D3641-qualified test data) against the lot the process was originally set up against — a material-lot shrinkage difference can mimic a process problem.
Check whether packing-phase pressure/time has drifted from the qualified setup sheet — under-packing is a common, distinct-from-cooling cause of shrinkage-related dimensional drift.

recommended_actions.action: Check cooling-channel flow rate and temperature uniformity across the mold; a partially blocked cooling channel is a common, easily-missed warpage cause.
Verify the current resin lot's shrinkage-rate data against the qualification lot before adjusting any process parameter.

symptom_description: A process-safety indicator review is due, or a Tier 3/4 leading indicator (near-miss, demand on a safety system, maintenance backlog on a safety-critical asset) has moved before any Tier 1/2 actual loss-of-containment event has occurred.
root_cause_framework: API RP 754's four-tier indicator pyramid — the explicit point of tracking Tier 3/4 leading indicators is to act BEFORE a Tier 1/2 event, so a moving leading indicator is itself the finding, not a precursor to wait out.
diagnostic_steps: Classify the moved indicator by tier (Tier 1-2 = actual event, Tier 3-4 = near-miss/operating-discipline) before deciding urgency — a Tier 3/4 movement gets a management-of-change review, not a shrug.
Check whether maintenance_alerts concentration on safety-critical-tagged equipment specifically (versus general equipment) is driving the leading-indicator movement.
Cross-reference major_audit_nonconformances for the same asset/unit to see whether this is a first occurrence or part of a pattern the last audit cycle already flagged.

recommended_actions.action: Review the specific operating procedure/permit-to-work step associated with the leading-indicator event; a Tier 3/4 movement is API RP 754's explicit signal to intervene at the procedure level before it becomes a Tier 1/2 event.

provenance.license_note: Full recommended practice is a licensed API publication; this is a structural summary only

symptom_description: A quality-control laboratory test result has come back out-of-specification (OOS) for a pharmaceutical batch or in-process sample.
root_cause_framework: FDA's 1999 OOS Guidance ("Investigating Out-of-Specification (OOS) Test Results for Pharmaceutical Production") + ICH Q7 lab-controls expectations — a two-phase investigation (Phase 1: laboratory error investigation; Phase 2: full manufacturing/process investigation) is required before an OOS result can be invalidated, and it CANNOT be invalidated on retesting alone.
diagnostic_steps: Phase 1 first, always: investigate for a laboratory error (technique, equipment calibration, sample handling) BEFORE any retest — retesting without a documented Phase 1 investigation is a common, citable FDA finding on its own.

If Phase 1 finds no assignable lab cause, escalate to Phase 2 (manufacturing/process investigation) — do not average an OOS result with subsequent passing retests to reach a passing conclusion; that practice is explicitly disallowed by the guidance.
Cross-reference first_pass_yield_by_stage for the same batch/stage to see whether the OOS result correlates with a specific process stage, supporting a Phase 2 manufacturing cause.

recommended_actions.action: Document the Phase 1 laboratory investigation fully (analyst, equipment, reagents, technique) before any retest is authorized — this documentation is what an auditor checks first.
If Phase 2 is triggered, hold the batch pending the full manufacturing investigation outcome; do not release on a favorable retest alone.

symptom_description: A return-pattern review (see the consumer-products return-pattern playbook) has identified a genuine defect-coded cluster large or severe enough to raise the question of whether a recall or corrective-action notice is warranted.
root_cause_framework: CPSC 16 CFR Part 1115 (Substantial Product Hazard Reports) + ISO 10377 traceability guidance — the binding regulatory question (is this reportable to CPSC within the statutory window) sits on top of the voluntary quality-pattern question the return-pattern playbook already answers.
diagnostic_steps: Determine whether the defect-coded cluster meets 16 CFR Part 1115's substantial-hazard reporting criteria (a legal/compliance determination, not a quality-team-only call) — this has a statutory reporting clock once triggered, unlike a routine quality review.
Verify lot/batch traceability depth for the affected SKU — confirm which specific production lots/date ranges the defect-coded returns actually trace back to before scoping any corrective action.

Cross-reference capa_closure_rate for this SKU's quality history — a pattern of open, slow-closing CAPAs on the same SKU strengthens the case for treating this as systemic rather than an isolated cluster.

recommended_actions.action: Route to legal/compliance for a 16 CFR Part 1115 reportability determination immediately — this decision has a statutory clock and should not wait on the full root-cause investigation to complete.
Verify lot-code traceability actually resolves to the affected production window before scoping which inventory/customers are in the corrective-action population.

symptom_description: Warranty claims or field-failure reports are rising for an industrial-products asset already in service at a customer site.
root_cause_framework: ISO 55001 asset-management feedback-loop requirement + Reliability-Centered Maintenance (RCM) failure-mode feedback — a field failure on higher-cost, longer-lived equipment is expected to feed back into both the manufacturer's design/process improvement AND the customer's own maintenance-planning assumptions, not just close as an isolated warranty transaction.
diagnostic_steps: Classify the field failure by failure mode (design, manufacturing, installation, or customer-side maintenance/misuse) before attributing cost or corrective action — RCM treats these as requiring different corrective paths.

Check whether this asset class shows a maintenance_alerts pattern internally (during production/test) that foreshadowed the field failure mode — a matched internal signal strengthens a manufacturing/design root cause versus a customer-side one.

Review whether the failure rate is consistent with the asset's designed service life at this point in its lifecycle, or is an early/unexpected failure — ISO 55001's lifecycle view treats these very differently.

recommended_actions.action: Cross-reference the failed unit's production-period quality data (scrap_rate, control_limit_deviations) to check whether an internal signal was already present and missed at the time of production.

Feed the failure mode back into the design/engineering change process per ISO 55001's continual-improvement requirement — a warranty closure alone does not satisfy the asset-management feedback-loop expectation.
